```{r setup}
library(meta5number)
has_mf <- requireNamespace("metafor", quietly = TRUE)  # the random-effects fits
```

```{r helpers, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
# a number for the prose, or "(not run)" where its chunk did not run
num <- function(x, d = 1, ok = TRUE) {
  if (ok) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d) else "(not run)"
}
```

## What the two examples show

This vignette assumes that the reader knows what `se_imputed_diff()` returns: each group's
mean and SD, imputed or sample, and each study's effect estimate with its naive and its exact
standard error, in the columns that `vignette("meta5number")` describes. Start there if the
columns, the scenarios or the conventions are new.

Wu, Shi and Tong (2026) apply the exact standard errors to two meta-analyses of COVID-19
patients, and this vignette runs both with the package. The first compares the mean blood urea
nitrogen (BUN) of patients in intensive care (ICU) with that of the other patients. The second
compares the variability of hemoglobin in the same two groups. In both, most studies report
the three quartiles of each group in place of a sample mean and SD.

We run each meta-analysis twice: with the naive standard errors, which treat the imputed mean
and SD as a sample mean and SD, and with the exact standard errors, which this package
computes from the exact standard deviation of the imputed mean and SD under normality. The
two runs share each study's effect
estimate $y_i$ and differ only in its variance $v_i$. The examples show three things:

- The pooled estimate changes little, by less than 5% in each of the four pairs of fits.

- The estimated heterogeneity falls, because the larger within-study variances $v_i$ leave
  less of the spread of the $y_i$ to be attributed to heterogeneity between studies.

- The standard error of the pooled estimate can rise or fall, depending on the model, and in
  the hemoglobin example the inference of the random-effects analysis is sensitive to which
  variances are used.

How large these changes are depends on the data. The examples illustrate the methodology, and
they do not establish clinical conclusions. Every number in this vignette is computed when
the vignette is built.

## The data

The study summaries ship with this package as the data sets `bun_icu` and `hgb_icu`. They come
from the systematic review of Katzenschlager et al. (2021) and are the data frames that
McGrath et al. (2023) published with their article. Group 1 (the columns ending in `.g1`) is
the ICU group and group 2 (`.g2`) the non-ICU group, as the data classify the patients. A
study reports the three quartiles of each group, or a sample mean and SD.

```{r data}
bun_icu[, 1:7]   # the ICU group; the non-ICU columns end in .g2
```

## Screening the studies by a skewness test

The imputed mean and SD, and their exact standard errors, rest on the assumption that the
data of a group are normal. Before imputing, we therefore apply the skewness test of Shi et
al. (2023) to every group that reports the three quartiles $q_1$, $q_2$, $q_3$ with its sample
size $n$. At the 5% level, the test rejects normality when
$$
|T| > \frac{2.65}{\sqrt n} - \frac{6}{n^2}, \qquad
T = \frac{q_1 + q_3 - 2 q_2}{q_3 - q_1},
$$
where the right-hand side is their approximate critical value. A study that reports the
sample mean and SD of both groups enters the analysis directly. Any other study enters only
if the test does not reject normality in either of its groups.

```{r screen}
# TRUE when the skewness test rejects normality in a group that reports the
# three quartiles, FALSE when it does not, or when the group reports a mean
# and SD
rejects <- function(q1, med, q3, n) {
  stat <- abs(q1 + q3 - 2 * med) / (q3 - q1)
  !is.na(stat) & stat > 2.65 / sqrt(n) - 6 / n^2
}
# a study is kept when neither of its groups is rejected
keep <- function(d) {
  !rejects(d$q1.g1, d$med.g1, d$q3.g1, d$n.g1) &
    !rejects(d$q1.g2, d$med.g2, d$q3.g2, d$n.g2)
}
bun <- bun_icu[keep(bun_icu), ]
hgb <- hgb_icu[keep(hgb_icu), ]
c(BUN = nrow(bun), hemoglobin = nrow(hgb))   # the studies that are pooled
```

```{r screen-numbers, echo = FALSE}
n_bun <- c(all = nrow(bun_icu), kept = nrow(bun))
n_hgb <- c(all = nrow(hgb_icu), kept = nrow(hgb))
# the prose below states these counts in words
stopifnot(n_bun["all"] == 7, n_bun["kept"] == 5, n_hgb["all"] == 7, n_hgb["kept"] == 7)
```

The test rejects normality in two of the seven BUN studies, which leaves five, and in none of
the seven hemoglobin studies.

## The two models

Both examples fit a common-effect model and a random-effects model. Study $i$ gives an effect
estimate $y_i$ with variance $v_i$, and the pooled estimate and its standard error are
$$
\hat\theta = \frac{\sum_i w_i y_i}{\sum_i w_i}, \qquad
\mathrm{SE}(\hat\theta) = \Big(\sum_i w_i\Big)^{-1/2}, \qquad
w_i = \frac{1}{v_i + \hat\tau^2},
$$
where $\hat\tau^2 = 0$ in the common-effect model, and in the random-effects model
$\hat\tau^2$ is the restricted maximum likelihood (REML) estimate of the between-study
variance. The 95% confidence interval is $\hat\theta \pm 1.96\,\mathrm{SE}(\hat\theta)$, a
normal approximation. The function `pool_imputed()` fits the common-effect model twice from
the output of `se_imputed_diff()`, once with the naive and once with the exact standard
errors, and prints the two fits side by side. The random-effects fits below use the `metafor`
package (Viechtbauer, 2010), which takes the columns `yi`, `sei_naive` and `sei` as they are.
We report the heterogeneity by $\hat\tau^2$ and by the index $I^2$, the share of the total
variation of the $y_i$ that is attributed to heterogeneity, in percent.

```{r reml}
# the REML random-effects fit under each standard error: the pooled estimate
# with its 95% confidence interval, its standard error, tau^2, and I^2 in
# percent as metafor reports it. The control settings tighten the iteration,
# so that an estimate of tau^2 at its lower bound comes out as 0.
fit_reml <- function(d) {
  ctrl <- list(tau2.init = 0, stepadj = 0.25, maxiter = 1000,
               threshold = 1e-10)
  one <- function(se) {
    f <- metafor::rma(yi = d$yi, sei = se, method = "REML", test = "z",
                      control = ctrl)
    c(estimate = as.numeric(f$b), ci.lb = f$ci.lb, ci.ub = f$ci.ub,
      se = f$se, tau2 = f$tau2, I2 = f$I2)
  }
  rbind(naive = one(d$sei_naive), exact = one(d$sei))
}
```

## The mean difference of BUN

The effect estimate of a study is the difference of the two groups' means, ICU minus non-ICU,
in mmol/L. For a group that reports the quartiles, the mean is the imputed mean, the best
linear unbiased estimator (BLUE) of the population mean from the three quartiles, and for a
group that reports its sample mean, it is that sample mean. The naive standard error of an
imputed mean is $\hat\sigma/\sqrt n$ and its exact standard error is $C_\mu(n)\,\hat\sigma$,
where $\hat\sigma$ is the imputed SD and $C_\mu(n)$ is the standard deviation of the imputed
mean in units of the population SD $\sigma$, at the group's own sample size $n$. The variance
$v_i$ is the sum of the two groups' squared standard errors. In the output below,
`scenario.g1` is `S2` for a group that reports the three quartiles and `sample` for a group
that reports a sample mean and SD, and `sei_naive` and `sei` are $\sqrt{v_i}$ under the naive
and the exact calculation.

```{r bun}
d_bun <- se_imputed_diff(bun)   # the difference of means, ICU minus non-ICU
print(d_bun[, c("author", "scenario.g1", "yi", "sei_naive", "sei")],
      digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
ce_bun <- pool_imputed(d_bun)   # the common-effect model
ce_bun
```

```{r bun-reml, eval = has_mf}
re_bun <- fit_reml(d_bun)       # the random-effects model
round(re_bun, 4)
```

```{r bun-numbers, echo = FALSE}
up <- function(f) 100 * (f["exact", "se"] / f["naive", "se"] - 1)   # change of the SE, percent
fb <- ce_bun$fits
imp_bun <- d_bun$scenario.g1 == "S2"
ratio_bun <- range((d_bun$sei / d_bun$sei_naive)[imp_bun])
if (!has_mf) re_bun <- matrix(NA_real_, 2, 6, dimnames = list(c("naive", "exact"),
                              c("estimate", "ci.lb", "ci.ub", "se", "tau2", "I2")))
# the prose below states these directions, so the build stops if the data no
# longer support them
stopifnot(ratio_bun[1] > 1, fb["exact", "se"] > fb["naive", "se"],
          all(fb[, "ci.lb"] > 0))
if (has_mf) stopifnot(re_bun["exact", "se"] < re_bun["naive", "se"],
                      re_bun["exact", "tau2"] < re_bun["naive", "tau2"],
                      re_bun["exact", "I2"] < re_bun["naive", "I2"],
                      all(re_bun[, "ci.lb"] > 0))
```

For the four studies with imputed means, the exact standard error of the difference is
`r num(100 * (ratio_bun[1] - 1))`% to `r num(100 * (ratio_bun[2] - 1))`% larger than the naive
one. The pooled mean difference is nearly the same under the two calculations:
`r num(fb["naive", "estimate"], 3)` and `r num(fb["exact", "estimate"], 3)` mmol/L under the
common-effect model, and `r num(re_bun["naive", "estimate"], 3, has_mf)` and
`r num(re_bun["exact", "estimate"], 3, has_mf)` mmol/L under the random-effects model. All
four confidence intervals lie above zero.

The two calculations differ mainly in the estimated heterogeneity. In the random-effects
fit, $\hat\tau^2$ falls from `r num(re_bun["naive", "tau2"], 4, has_mf)` (mmol/L)$^2$ under
the naive standard errors to `r num(re_bun["exact", "tau2"], 4, has_mf)` under the exact
ones, and $I^2$, as `metafor` reports it for this fit, from
`r num(re_bun["naive", "I2"], 1, has_mf)`% to `r num(re_bun["exact", "I2"], 1, has_mf)`%.
The standard error of the pooled difference moves in opposite directions under the two
models. Under the common-effect model, the larger $v_i$ reduce the total weight, and the
standard error rises by `r num(up(fb))`%. Under the random-effects model, the fall of
$\hat\tau^2$ more than offsets the larger $v_i$, and the standard error falls by
`r num(-up(re_bun), 1, has_mf)`%.

## The SD ratio of hemoglobin

A meta-analysis of variability asks whether an outcome is more dispersed in one group than in
another. The effect estimate is the log of the ratio of the two groups' SDs, each imputed or,
where the study reports it, the sample SD,
$y_i = \log(\hat\sigma_{1i}/\hat\sigma_{2i})$, the log variability ratio of Nakagawa et al.
(2015) without its small-sample correction term, as in Wu, Shi and Tong (2026). The argument
`measure = "lnVR"` of `se_imputed_diff()` gives $y_i$ with its two standard errors in place of
the difference of means. The pooled estimate and the limits of its confidence interval are exponentiated to
give the pooled SD ratio.

The variance of $y_i$ is the sum of one term per group, to first order in each group's SD
(the delta method). The naive calculation gives every group the term of a sample SD of $n$
normal observations, $1/\{2(n - 1)\}$. The exact calculation keeps that term for a group that
reports its sample SD and uses $C^2_\sigma(n)$, the exact variance of the imputed SD in units
of $\sigma^2$, where $\sigma$ is the group's population SD, for a group whose SD is imputed
from the quartiles.

```{r hgb}
d_hgb <- se_imputed_diff(hgb, measure = "lnVR")
print(d_hgb[, c("author", "scenario.g1", "yi", "sei_naive", "sei")],
      digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
ce_hgb <- pool_imputed(d_hgb)   # the common-effect model, on the log scale
ce_hgb
```

```{r hgb-reml, eval = has_mf}
re_hgb <- fit_reml(d_hgb)       # the random-effects model, on the log scale
# the pooled SD ratio with its 95% confidence interval
round(exp(re_hgb[, c("estimate", "ci.lb", "ci.ub")]), 3)
round(re_hgb[, c("se", "tau2", "I2")], 4)
```

```{r hgb-numbers, echo = FALSE}
fh <- ce_hgb$fits
imp_hgb <- d_hgb$scenario.g1 == "S2" & d_hgb$scenario.g2 == "S2"
n_imp_hgb <- c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven")[sum(imp_hgb)]
ratio_hgb <- range((d_hgb$sei / d_hgb$sei_naive)[imp_hgb]^2)
if (!has_mf) re_hgb <- re_bun
sr <- exp(re_hgb[, c("estimate", "ci.lb", "ci.ub")])   # the random-effects SD ratio
ce_sr <- exp(fh[, c("estimate", "ci.lb", "ci.ub")])    # the common-effect SD ratio
# the prose below states these facts, so the build stops if the data no longer
# support them
stopifnot(ratio_hgb[1] > 1, fh["exact", "se"] > fh["naive", "se"],
          all(ce_sr[, "ci.lb"] > 1))
if (has_mf) stopifnot(re_hgb["naive", "tau2"] > 0, re_hgb["exact", "tau2"] < 1e-8,
                      sr["naive", "ci.lb"] < 1, sr["exact", "ci.lb"] > 1,
                      isTRUE(all.equal(unname(sr["exact", ]), unlist(ce_sr["exact", ]),
                                       check.attributes = FALSE, tolerance = 1e-6)))
# the overview says that the pooled estimate changes by less than 5% in each of
# the four pairs of fits (the SD ratio on its own scale)
rel <- function(a, b) abs(b / a - 1)
stopifnot(rel(fb["naive", "estimate"], fb["exact", "estimate"]) < 0.05,
          rel(ce_sr["naive", "estimate"], ce_sr["exact", "estimate"]) < 0.05)
if (has_mf) stopifnot(rel(re_bun["naive", "estimate"], re_bun["exact", "estimate"]) < 0.05,
                      rel(sr["naive", "estimate"], sr["exact", "estimate"]) < 0.05)
```

For each of the `r n_imp_hgb` studies whose two SDs are imputed from the quartiles, the exact
variance $v_i$ is `r num(ratio_hgb[1], 2)` to `r num(ratio_hgb[2], 2)` times the naive one. Under the
common-effect model, the standard error of the pooled log ratio rises by `r num(up(fh))`%, and
both confidence intervals of the SD ratio lie above 1. Under the random-effects model,
$\hat\tau^2$ falls from `r num(re_hgb["naive", "tau2"], 4, has_mf)` under the naive standard
errors to `r num(re_hgb["exact", "tau2"], 0, has_mf)` under the exact ones. With
$\hat\tau^2 = 0$, the random-effects model has the weights of the common-effect model, so the
two models give the same pooled SD ratio under the exact standard errors.

Under the random-effects model, the pooled SD ratio is `r num(sr["naive", "estimate"], 3, has_mf)`
(`r num(sr["naive", "ci.lb"], 3, has_mf)`, `r num(sr["naive", "ci.ub"], 3, has_mf)`) with the
naive standard errors and `r num(sr["exact", "estimate"], 3, has_mf)`
(`r num(sr["exact", "ci.lb"], 3, has_mf)`, `r num(sr["exact", "ci.ub"], 3, has_mf)`) with the
exact ones. The naive interval includes 1, and the exact interval does not. The two results
differ only through the within-study variances $v_i$, so the inference is sensitive to how
these variances are calculated.

The plot below shows each study's SD ratio with its 95% confidence interval under the two
calculations. The exact interval is wider for every study with imputed SDs and the same for
the two studies that report their sample SDs.

```{r forest, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2, fig.alt = "Forest plot of the hemoglobin SD ratios of seven studies, each with a naive and an exact 95% confidence interval. The exact interval is wider for the five studies with imputed SDs."}
est <- exp(d_hgb$yi)
z <- qnorm(0.975)
half <- cbind(naive = z * d_hgb$sei_naive, exact = z * d_hgb$sei)
lab <- sub(" \\(.*$", "", d_hgb$author)   # the first author
k <- nrow(d_hgb)
op <- par(mar = c(4, 11, 1, 1))
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, max(exp(d_hgb$yi + half))), ylim = c(0.5, k + 0.5),
     yaxt = "n", ylab = "", xlab = "Hemoglobin SD ratio, ICU / non-ICU")
axis(2, at = k:1, labels = lab, las = 1, tick = FALSE)
abline(v = 1, lty = 3)
for (v in 1:2) {                          # 1 the naive interval, 2 the exact
  y <- k:1 + c(0.15, -0.15)[v]
  segments(exp(d_hgb$yi - half[, v]), y, exp(d_hgb$yi + half[, v]), y,
           lty = c(2, 1)[v])
  points(est, y, pch = c(22, 24)[v], bg = c("white", "black")[v])
}
legend("bottomright", legend = c("naive", "exact"), lty = c(2, 1),
       pch = c(22, 24), pt.bg = c("white", "black"), bty = "n")
par(op)
```

```{r not-run, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
# printed only when metafor was missing at build time, so the numbers of the
# random-effects fits read "(not run)"
if (!has_mf) cat("The package metafor was not available when this vignette was",
                 "built, so the random-effects fits did not run. Install it",
                 "and rebuild the vignette, or run the calls above in a",
                 "session that has it.\n")
```

```{r check, include = FALSE}
# pool_imputed() and metafor agree on the common-effect fit
if (has_mf) {
  f <- metafor::rma(yi, sei = sei, data = d_bun, method = "EE")
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(c(as.numeric(f$b), f$se),
                             unlist(fb["exact", c("estimate", "se")], use.names = FALSE))))
}
```

Katzenschlager S, Zimmer AJ, Gottschalk C, Grafeneder J, Schmitz S, Kraker S, Ganslmeier M,
Muth A, Seitel A, Maier-Hein L, Benedetti A, Larmann J, Weigand MA, McGrath S, Denkinger CM
(2021). Can we predict the severe course of
COVID-19 - a systematic review and meta-analysis of indicators of clinical outcome? PLOS ONE
16(7), e0255154.

McGrath S, Katzenschlager S, Zimmer AJ, Seitel A, Steele R, Benedetti A (2023). Standard error
estimation in meta-analysis of studies reporting medians. Statistical Methods in Medical
Research 32(2), 373-388.

Nakagawa S, Poulin R, Mengersen K, Reinhold K, Engqvist L, Lagisz M, Senior AM (2015).
Meta-analysis of variation: ecological and evolutionary applications and beyond. Methods in
Ecology and Evolution 6(2), 143-152.

Shi J, Luo D, Wan X, Liu Y, Liu J, Bian Z, Tong T (2023). Detecting the skewness of data from
the five-number summary and its application in meta-analysis. Statistical Methods in Medical
Research 32(7), 1338-1360.

Viechtbauer W (2010). Conducting meta-analyses in R with the metafor package. Journal of
Statistical Software 36(3), 1-48.

Wu Z, Shi J, Tong T (2026). Precision of the imputed mean and standard deviation from the
five-number summary. Manuscript.
